prime.problem: Interview notes are copied, trusted and memorised. If a line of code crashes, mutates its input or answers the wrong question, you learn the bug along with the idea and repeat it in the interview.
prime.fits: The second card of the map. It builds on the overview's source-to-course table: the errors are grouped by the same courses, and the cards written from references have no rows because there was nothing to check.
expect: four kinds of error (crash, wrong answer, silent, stated backwards)
"ran it", "compiled" and "brute force" as checking methods
wrong but silent: mutation, leaks, reading memory it shouldn't
where errors cluster in hand-kept notes
prime.goal: Sort any source error into one of the four kinds, say which checking method would have caught it, and explain why silent errors and one-line paper summaries are the riskiest parts of notes like these.

attend: Why is a silent error (the LFU count map, the caller's list growing by one 0 per call) more dangerous in an interview than code that won't compile?
Cheapest Flights runs Prim and returns 400 instead of 700. What was the source's algorithm actually optimising, and which inputs did it never read?
Newton's square root is wrong on only 3 of 2³¹ inputs. What checking method finds that, and why would random testing likely miss it?
Why does the card put "right answer, assumption unstated" in a separate list instead of counting those as errors?
Most cs-3 rows are name errors and most cs-5/cs-6 rows are paper summaries stated backwards. What does each cluster say about how the notes were written?

must: Code that was never run → names used outside their scope, missing colons, undefined helpers → it crashes on first use → cheap to catch (just run it) → which is why crashes are the biggest group (11) and most of cs-3's rows

A function that changes its argument (heights.append(0), board.pop()) or forgets to clean up (the LFU count map) → the returned answer is still right → example-based tests pass → the bug only shows on repeated calls or in memory → you need an invariant or a check of the input after the call

A one-line summary of a long paper → a qualifier gets flipped ("no" → "most" queues, truncation "guarantees" catch-up) → the claim reads fine and nothing crashes → only the paper itself can catch it → treat one-line paper summaries as leads to verify, not facts

Compare with a slow, obviously correct version on many random inputs → any disagreement is a bug, whatever kind it is → but a bug that fires on only a few inputs (3 of 2³¹ for Newton) needs exhaustive or targeted edge tests, not random ones
elevated: Code that relies on unspecified C++ evaluation order (swap(a[j], a[--j])) happens to work under clang → it can break under another compiler or flag → listed as unclear, not wrong, because no run produced a wrong answer
reference: the exact tallies: 30 errors on 27 cards; 11 / 8 / 5 / 6 by kind
the toolchain: Python 3.10, Apple clang 17, M3
the full list of typos and mislabels

compress.prompt: Without scrolling up, write the four kinds of error as four short lines, each with one example and the check that catches it. Then add one sentence on where the errors cluster and why.
checklist: crash or won't compile: caught by running or compiling it (radix sort's arr vs array)
wrong answer: caught by an exact calculation or a brute force (Prim for shortest path: 400 vs 700)
silent: caught by an invariant or by checking the input after the call (LFU leak, mutated list)
stated backwards: caught only by reading the paper or a textbook (QJUMP queues, Bayou truncation, insertion sort vs quicksort)
clusters: unrun code (cs-3) and one-line paper summaries (cs-5, cs-6)
most of the source is right: 154 of 181 cards need no correction

retrieve.q: Explain why the card counts "a right answer with an unstated assumption" and "C++ that works by luck" separately from the 30 real errors.
answer: an error must change an answer or fail a run
unstated assumptions give the right answer under the intended reading
evaluation-order code is correct under clang; it's a portability risk, not a wrong result
counting them would inflate the error rate and blur what to actually fix

retrieve.q: Walk through what happens when the source's monotonic-stack function is called three times on the same list [2, 1, 5].
answer: each call appends the sentinel 0 to the caller's list
the answer is right each time, since one extra 0 at the end changes no area
after three calls the list is [2, 1, 5, 0, 0, 0]
fix: work on heights + [0], so the input is left alone

retrieve.q: You have time for one checking method on a new set of notes: run every snippet, or compare each against a brute force. Which do you pick, and what does each one miss?
answer: running catches the largest group (crashes) cheaply but misses wrong answers and silent bugs
brute force catches wrong answers and some silent ones, but costs a second implementation per problem
neither catches a paper stated backwards; that needs the source paper
neither reliably catches a bug on 3 of 2³¹ inputs; that needs exhaustive or edge-targeted tests

retrieve.q: Explain why the Cheapest Flights solution returns a plausible-looking number instead of crashing, and why that makes it harder to catch.
answer: Prim builds a minimum spanning tree over the whole graph and returns its weight
it never reads src, dst or k, so it answers a different question
a number comes back, so nothing looks broken
only comparing against a correct shortest path with at most k stops (Bellman–Ford, k + 1 rounds: 700) exposes it

compare.q: This card's checking methods vs that card's testing ladder (hand trace, edge cases, random vs brute force, invariant): which rung would have caught each kind of source error?
answer: hand trace or running once: crashes and name errors
random vs brute force: wrong answers such as the Prim swap
an invariant on internal state: silent leaks such as the LFU count map (46.7% of random cases broke it on that card)
no test rung catches a paper stated backwards; that needs the source

compare.q: Prim's minimum spanning tree vs a shortest path with at most k stops: what does each optimise, and why can one never stand in for the other?
answer: MST: cheapest set of edges connecting all nodes, with no start or end
shortest path: cheapest route from src to dst, here capped at k + 1 edges
an MST path between two nodes can be far from the cheapest route
use MST for network build cost; use Bellman–Ford or Dijkstra for routes

compare.q: The overview lists 49 cards as written from references; this card lists 30 errors. Why do the reference-written courses (cs-7, cs-10) have no rows here, and does that make them more trustworthy?
answer: their source headings were empty, so there was no source claim to be wrong
no rows means "nothing to check", not "checked and right"
their correctness rests on the references each footer names and on the series' own runs

predict.q: The source says Y ~ U(0, 5) and asks for P(4x² + 4xY + Y + 2 = 0 has real roots). Before working it out: is the source's 2/5 too high or too low, and roughly what should a million-draw simulation print?
predict.answer: Too low. Real roots need the discriminant 16Y² − 16(Y + 2) ≥ 0, i.e. (Y − 2)(Y + 1) ≥ 0, so Y ≥ 2 on (0, 5): probability 3/5. The source kept (0, 2), where the roots are complex. A 10⁶-draw simulation prints about 0.600 (one seeded run gave 0.6006).

apply.task: Pick two rows of different kinds and reproduce them in Python. (1) Silent: write the source-style largest_rectangle that does heights.append(0), call it three times on [2, 1, 5], and print the list afterwards. (2) Wrong answer: simulate Y ~ U(0, 5) a million times and count how often 4x² + 4xY + Y + 2 has real roots. For each, name the check that caught it.
apply.done: The list prints [2, 1, 5, 0, 0, 0] (fixed by using heights + [0]), and the simulation lands near 0.6 (exact 3/5), not the source's 0.4; you named "inspect the input after the call" for the first and "exact answer vs simulation" for the second.
apply.hint: Real roots when the discriminant b² − 4ac ≥ 0, with a = 4, b = 4Y, c = Y + 2.
